pages.title: WELCOME TO LATIN ROOTS
content: More than half of English is Latin, and
nearly all of its long words are: the
language of law, science, government and
the essay. Salary, muscle, pencil, money
and candidate are Latin. So is computer.
Most of them are built from parts. Learn
a part once and every word that carries it
opens: port is carry, so transport, export
and portable are carry-across, carry-out
and carry-able before you look them up.
This pack teaches the parts, root by root,
and two words on every card: the headword
and a relative. You need no Latin. You
need to notice.

pages.title: HOW A CARD WORKS
content: The front shows a word. Press a key and the
card opens in stages: a sentence that uses
it, its DEFINITION, a second example built
on a RELATIVE of the same root, and, on 8,
the notes.
The relative is the second word on the
card: submarine brings marine, candidate
brings candid. Five hundred cards, a
thousand words. The notes show the parts
and what each part means, with the Latin:
sub- (under) + MARINE (Latin mare, sea)
Rate the card 0 to 5 when it is open. The
boss fight asks the definition and offers
eight words; the synonyms and antonyms in
the notes are the clues you take with you.
THE FIRST TWENTY are the famous ones:
aquarium, submarine, candidate, salary,
muscle, pencil, money, vaccine. Each comes
apart in the hand, and each carries one
line of its story: the white toga, the
little mouse, the salt allowance.
THEN the words English took from Latin
whole (agenda, alibi, bonus, virus), then
the toolkit of prefixes, then the roots,
two to a cluster: port and mit, carry and
send; dict and scrib, say and write.
Every cluster opens with a short lesson
naming its parts. Tier 5 is the pack's
advanced register, one root at a time.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: the famous twenty.
These words came into English whole, not
built from parts. Several are a complete
Latin sentence in one word.
exit      he goes out
video     I see
audio     I hear
agenda    things to be done
Latin puts the person in the verb ending:
videre is to see, video is I see. Data and
agenda are Latin plurals; English treats
each as one thing.
Computer is the odd one: it meant a person
hired to do arithmetic until the 1940s.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: Latin taken whole.
A prefix goes on the front and sets the
direction. The root says what is done.
ex-     out        re-     back
in-     into       de-     down
con-    together   dis-    apart
trans-  across     ob-     against
sub-    under      per-    through
super-  above      circum- around
inter-  between    contra- opposite
pre-    before     ab-     away
post-   after      ad-     toward
pro-    forward    se-     aside
in- is two prefixes in one spelling: into
(influx) and not (invisible). ad- hides in
accept, affix and arrive.
THE NEXT 20 CARDS: the prefixes.
PORT (Latin portare) means carry. MIT
(Latin mittere, missus) means send, let go.
transport   across + carry
export      out + carry
transmit    across + send
permit      through + let go
Read an unknown word in three pieces: the
prefix gives the direction, the root gives
the meaning, the suffix gives the part of
speech. ex + port + able: out, carry, able
to be.
A mission is a sending, a missile a thing
sent. The harbor port is Latin portus, a
different word.
THE NEXT 19 CARDS: port and mit words.
DICT (Latin dicere, to say) means say.
SCRIB and its past form SCRIPT (Latin
scribere, to write) mean write.
predict     before + say
contradict  against + say
describe    down + write
postscript  after + written
A verdict is a true saying: ver- is Latin
verus, true. A benediction is a blessing,
a well-saying, from bene, well.
Indict is said as indite. The silent c was
put back into the spelling to show the
Latin dicere underneath.
THE NEXT 18 CARDS: dict and scrib words.
DUC, also DUCT (Latin ducere, to lead),
means lead. TRACT (Latin trahere, tractus,
to pull) means pull or drag.
produce     forward + lead
reduce      back + lead
extract     out + pull
contract    together + pull
An aqueduct leads water. A duke leads men:
Latin dux, a leader, is the same root.
Educate is lead out, not fill up: e- (out)
and ducere, to draw what is in the pupil
into the open.
THE NEXT 18 CARDS: duc and tract words.
A suffix goes on the end and tells you
what kind of word you are holding: a noun,
an adjective, a verb.
-ion    act of        -ous      full of
-ment   result of     -ate      to make
-ance   state of      -ify      turn into
-ity    quality of    -escent   becoming
-or     one who       -escence  the process
-ory    place for     -ule      small
-able   able to be    -cle      little
-ive    tending to    -ulous    inclined to
-al     relating to   -itude    condition
-able and -ible are the same suffix in two
spellings, and so are -ance and -ence.
THE NEXT 19 CARDS: the suffixes.
